raised about a million dollars to make a business around an AI chatbot...

The name of that company? HuggingFace

The now infamous Attention is All you need transformers paper Google put out, the one that powered the current AI insanity we're living through right now, hadn't dropped yet....

That came out in 2017. So in 2016, for these 3 cofounders, their AI chatbot would have been technically limited,
think about how Alexa and Siri used to feel... that's what they would have been working with technology wise.

So when Google dropped their Transformers paper in 2017, and then more importantly a year later in 2018 Google released BERT, an open weights LLM.... well... you could say it got the attention of HuggingFace... to say the least

It's worth noting a lesser known company, dropped an open model by the name of GPT1 a little bit before Bert was released... both models followed the same basic formula.

A foundational model following the "Attention is all you need" architecture, followed with two stages of learning, phase one is unsupervised, you feed it blindly all the data you can, and phase two is supervised, you slowly, using humans back then, reinforce it to behave like you want it to... like a chat bot...
No one was really paying attention to OpenAI, but Bert was getting a lot of attention... here's an example of it in action, I ask it what the capital of New Jersey is, and it correctly says Newark.
I ask it what two plus two is equal to, and it correctly says the answer is One.

So for a company working on an AI chatbot? Well suffice to say they took notice...

They wanted to adopt Bert. Tweak it.. fine tune it... you mgiht even say transform it

And so they released pytorch pretrained bert version 0.1.1

That's a mouthful...

but importantly this became the foundation of the popular transformers library that's an industry standard for working with open source models today...

This represented a transition in the company's history, from a company focused on a single chatbot, to a company focused on providing the infrastructure that powers open source models

And so a couple years later, they launched the hub... a platform that now hosts all of the most popular open source models in the world, the code required to run them, as well as a lot of open training data

I want to introduce you to The Stack. This is a dataset on HuggingFace. It has 3 terrabytes of permissive code scraped from GitHub.

I'm going to tell you some stories about this data,

but what you have to keep in mind is there is no metaphor I can give you that really wraps your mind around how much data this is. And there isn't enough time in a million conference talks to tell you all the stories contained in this data.

They say one exposed key is a tragedy, well 70,000 is a statistic... so I'm going to take you on a journey showing you some of those individual tragedies...

But before I start telling you stories about the data... the first story I'm going to tell you... doesn't even occur on the hub... it strikes at the very definition of what open AI even means. Models aren't exactly source code.. so how can the source be open? is open source even the right word for an open model?
That question... almost tour an open source non-profit called the Open Source Initiative apart
Who even are the OSI? and why should you care? Well in the 90's their founder coined the term "Open Source"

And many governments for years recognize their definition of open source software...

Why does it matter how a government defines open source?
The short answer is regulation. Allow me to introduce you to the European AI act, which gives special carveouts to Open Source models, lowering their legal and compliance overhead burden
So why did this almost break the OSI? Disagreements over the definition of open-source when it comes to AI models... and at the heart of it? Data.
Should datasets, like the 880,000 datasets already hosted on huggingface, be a requirement in order to call an open source model, open source?

A question that was so charged, the OSI suspended their board election, because they didn't want a new board member with radical views on this topic... and the radical view in question? That the data should be open as part of the open-source defintion.

You can find the petition online containing hundreds of names, upset with this outcome... so why? Why resist open data as a part of open models? What is it about opening up the data that seems so impractical to the OSI board, they put themselves in this frankly embarrassing crossroads?

To answer that question... we need to zoom in on some of the data

In 1896 a british statesman Lord Rosebery was giving a series of widely attended political speeches across england...

There were no recording devices at the time... the only way to learn about the speeches was to send a reporter and have a reporter transcribe them

and that's exactly what The Times did.

The reporter followed rosenbery for a year, and documented verbatim transcripts which the paper published.

A book publisher wanted to make these more widely available.. John Lane took the transcripts from The Times and published them...

The Times sued him. Almost immediately.
It seems a little crazy right? That even though the information was public, the news paper could control that information... this was 120 years ago.

not much changed in 120 years...

that old illegal book from 120 years ago? I have a copy of it, and guess what? There's a word for word copy of it in thousands of AI training sets

I want to introduce you to another dataset on the hub..

Common Crawl.

Put simply, common crawl is a scrape of the entire internet

Common crawl is actually more than one scrape, it's a routine scrape, and each oneis 363 terrabytes.

By itself it's unfathomably large..

What happens... when the one of the millions of websites they crawl reaches out saying, "HEY! Don't include us in your data"

And what happens.. when that one, just so happens to be the new york times

Well... they comply with the request...

But what does that mean for open source models that trained on it? Is it impossible to recreate them now?

Whether we're talking about copyright... or security, or data privacy, some of these problems are frankly impossible to solve.

At least with our current technology

And that's what made the OSI election so explosive...

It wasn't a friendly debate about we should lower the bar for corporations to claim regulatory benefit...

It was actually a debate about whether for many of these models, could even legally, in a privacy friendly and secure way, possibly open their data.

And even if they could, to what end if random copyright owners could just slowly strike bits and pieces until the dataset looks completely different than the one that was used to generate the open weights

There are workarounds...

Let me introduce you to laion 5 billion...

A dataset of BILLIONS of images... except the dataset itself contains zero images.

The workaround?

The dataset just has links to external websites with the images.

It would be a nightmare to actually host these images, for all the reasons you're probably imagining...

But this doesn't solve all our problems. Those links? They're going to rot over time. And this dataset will slowly attrify over time the same way our hosted one with copyright strikes will...

We cannot look at open datasets the same way we look at open source software.

It's too different... the legal, privacy and security challenges are just... different. 

And let me put this into better perspective...

They say one leaked API key is a tragedy... millions of leaked API keys is a statistic...

Well here's an interesting fact, most of those 70,000 keys? They existed in more than one dataset.

Why?

Well imagine a key gets leaked on github... I shared multiple stories about different datasets containing keys from github...

A lot of these datasets scrape the same data.


One example that popped up a lot... was THOUSANDS of unique twitter API keys we found just over and over and over again in hundreds of datasets...

Why twitter? Well first is it's really easy to make tutorials out of twitter API keys. It's basically the only social media site with a well supported API.

The second reason was a surprising data curation bias we weren't expecting going in...

A lot of people pulled out of larger datasets, currated code that they would automate at scale, testing to make sure the code actually ran...

Well think about it. Code that hardcoded secrets would run without exception, but code that depends on secrets would throw exceptions...

This actually biased many datasets towards having hardcoded keys, and replicated the keys into multiple datasets...

And the last element here...

The first gen LLM's that learned the behavior, pushed more similiar data into the wild, creating a vicious cyclical feedback loop
And you can see examples of that here, copies of the same exact data, currated datasets, that are subsets of one another.

This got us thinking though.... so many keys shared because they got scraped and distilled from larger scrapes...

What about cases where data accidentally gets exposed?

That wouldn't show up in multiple scrapes it would be unique..

So of our 70,000 keys if we specifically filter for keys that are from exactly only one dataset...

maybe... just maybe...

That key wasn't from the public scrape, it was from accidental data that got packaged in....

It's a bold strategy... but it might just work...

So we tried it. And it did work. That's how we were able to bring you most of the examples we covered...

But even within the orphaned keys, there were hundreds, far too many to go through all of them..

That's how I was able to bring all of these stories to you though.


What about all theo ther keys though? The keys scraped from websites, github repositories, and chats that were publicly exposed outside of huggingface that huggingface just made copies of...

between legal security and private issues, there's a unique set of problems with opening up datasets, and with datasets that are already open...

in 100 years, are tehse huge collections of data going to tell our story?
